questions.question: When are events $A$ and $B$ conditionally independent given $C$?
What condition is required for conditioning on $C$?
What does conditional independence mean intuitively?
options: Two events cannot happen at the same time
Two events stop influencing each other once certain information is known
Two events are independent before any information is known

questions.question: Is conditional independence the same as ordinary independence?
options: Yes, they always mean exactly the same thing
Yes, ordinary independence always implies conditional independence

questions.question: Where is conditional independence especially central?
Two symptoms are dependent overall but independent given disease status. Which concept describes this?
If $P(A\mid C)=0.4$, $P(B\mid C)=0.5$, and $A,B$ are conditionally independent given $C$, what is $P(A\cap B\mid C)$?
Two students' answers become independent once their preparation levels are known. What is the condition being controlled for?
options: The event that both answers are identical

questions.question: Machine failures in different locations may be conditionally independent given what?
If $P(A\cap B\mid C)=0.12$, $P(A\mid C)=0.3$, and $P(B\mid C)=0.4$, are $A$ and $B$ conditionally independent given $C$?
options: No, because all conditional probabilities differ
No, because conditional independence is disjointness

questions.question: Why can marginal dependence coexist with conditional independence?
options: Ordinary independence implies every event has probability zero.
A common cause creates association that disappears after conditioning on it.

questions.question: What does 'inside a restricted situation' refer to in conditional independence?
options: All events outside $C$ get probability one
The sample space is ignored completely
The events are treated as ordered selections

questions.question: Which equality would show conditional independence of $A$ and $B$ given $C$ using $P(B\mid A\cap C)$?
options: $P(B\mid A\cap C)=P(A\mid C)$ always, mixing up $A$ and $B$.
$P(B\mid A\cap C)=P(B\mid C)$ when the terms are defined

questions.question: If $P(A\mid C)=0.2$, $P(B\mid C)=0.7$, and $P(A\cap B\mid C)=0.20$, are the events conditionally independent given $C$?
options: Yes, because all probabilities are positive
No, because conditional independence requires disjointness

questions.question: A hospital records two symptoms. They are associated overall, but after conditioning on disease status the association disappears. What is the best description?
options: The symptoms are disjoint, meaning they cannot occur together at all
The two symptoms are independent overall, which they are not
The symptoms are conditionally independent given disease status
The symptoms are complements, meaning one precludes the other

questions.question: If $P(C)=0$, what is the issue with asking whether $A$ and $B$ are conditionally independent given $C$?
Why does conditional independence not imply ordinary independence in general?
options: Ordinary independence is weaker than equality of probabilities
The event $C$ must be the full sample space
The factorization may hold only after restricting to $C$

questions.question: Two events can be marginally dependent yet conditionally independent. Which mechanism explains this pattern?
options: The events are impossible until the common cause is removed.
The shared factor makes all probabilities equal to one
A shared factor creates dependence; once known, no influence remains.
The events become complements after conditioning

questions.question: Given weather $C$, two location failures have probabilities $0.1$ and $0.2$ and are conditionally independent. What is the conditional probability that both fail?
If two answers are conditionally independent given preparation level $C$, with $P(A\mid C)=0.6$ and $P(B\mid C)=0.6$, what is $P(A\cap B\mid C)$?
